column1: She {{c1::goes}} to work by train every day. (go)
column2: goes | Use the present simple for routines. With she, add -es to go.

column1: They {{c1::were having}} dinner when I called. (have)
column2: were having | Use the past continuous for an action in progress when another happened.

column1: I {{c1::have read}} this book twice. (read)
column2: have read | Use the present perfect for experience without a stated time.

column1: If it rains, we {{c1::will stay}} at home. (stay)
column2: will stay | In a first conditional, use the present simple after if and will in the result.

column1: There {{c1::are}} two chairs in the room. (be)
column2: are | Use are with a plural noun.

column1: This exercise is {{c1::easier}} than the last one. (easy)
column2: easier | For short adjectives ending in y, change y to i and add -er.

column1: She has worked here {{c1::since}} 2020. (since / for)
column2: since | Use since with the starting point of a period.

column1: By the time we arrived, the film {{c1::had started}}. (start)
column2: had started | The past perfect marks an action completed before another past action.

column1: Please {{c1::switch off}} the lights when you leave. (switch / make)
column2: switch off | Switch off means to stop a device or light from operating.

column1: I need to {{c1::make}} an appointment with the dentist. (make / do)
column2: make | The usual expression is make an appointment.

column1: Could you {{c1::give}} me a hand with these bags? (give / take)
column2: give | Give someone a hand means help them.

column1: The opposite of “borrow” is {{c1::lend}}.
column2: lend | You borrow something from someone; you lend something to someone.

column1: The meeting was {{c1::put off}} until Friday. (put off / put on)
column2: put off | Put off means postpone.

column1: I’m looking {{c1::for}} my keys. I can’t find them. (for / after)
column2: for | Look for means search for something.

column1: “How are you?” “I’m well, {{c1::thanks}}.”
column2: thanks | Thanks is a natural response when someone asks how you are.

column1: “Could you repeat that, {{c1::please}}?”
column2: please | Please makes a request more polite.

column1: “Excuse me, how do I get {{c1::to}} the station?” (to / at)
column2: to | Use get to when asking about reaching a destination.

column1: “Would you like some tea?” “Yes, {{c1::please}}.”
column2: please | Yes, please is a polite way to accept an offer.

column1: “I’m sorry I’m late.” “That’s {{c1::okay}}.”
column2: okay | That’s okay is a common way to accept an apology.

column1: “Can I pay {{c1::by}} card?” (by / with a)
column2: by | Say pay by card, or pay with a card.
